en.g: ornamental embroidery; decorative needlework produced using any embroidery technique

46701.etyen:
From pryd (“ornament, decoration”) + søm (“sewing, stitching”), literally "ornamental stitching".
The first element is related to Old Norse prýði (“ornament, splendour”), from prúðr (“stately, splendid”), probably borrowed from Old English prūd (“proud, noble”). The second element continues Old Norse saumr (“stitch, seam”), from Proto-Germanic *saumaz (“stitch, seam, hem”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *syewH- (“to sew”).
Compare the equivalent Norwegian Nynorsk formation Norwegian Nynorsk prydsaum (“ornamental embroidery, decorative stitching”).

en.g: a male given name from Old Norse

1001325.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Sundri (“male given name”), of uncertain meaning. One interpretation analyses the Old Norse name as meaning “one of two”; another connects it with the Old Norse name element sunn- (“southern”).
The older form Sundri is documented in Norway from approximately 1340, particularly in eastern Norway. The modern name has traditionally been associated especially with Telemark.
Compare Danish Sondre and Swedish Sondre (“male given name”).

en.g: yuck, ew; an expression of disgust or revulsion
x: Han hopper på de svampete restene så de glir ut som søle under støvlene. Æsj, bæsj! roper han og ler.
He jumps on the spongy remains so that they spread like mud beneath his boots. “Yuck, ew!” he shouts and laughs.

1001581.etyen:
Probably after æsj (“yuck, ew”), an expressive imitative interjection used to express disgust or revulsion. Compare the similarly expressive Norwegian interjections isj, usj, fysj, øsj, and ysj.
The noun is a nominalization of the interjection.

1004653.etyen:
From ert (“pea”) + brød (“bread”), with linking -e- (“interfix”), literally “pea bread”. The first element, ert, is inherited from Old Norse ertr (“peas”), possibly ultimately from a Mediterranean language. The second element, brød, is the Danish-form word from Old Danish brøth (“bread”), corresponding to Old Norse brauð (“bread”) and dialectal Norwegian brau (“bread”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk ertebrød (“pea flatbread”).

en.g: onion; the cultivated plant Allium cepa, grown for its edible bulb

We grow onions and carrots in the vegetable garden.
Hageløk er et annet navn på kepaløk.

1005165.etyen:
Compound of hage (“garden”) + løk (“onion”), literally “garden onion”.
The first component, hage (“garden”), derives from Old Norse hagi (“pasture, enclosure”), from Proto-Germanic *hagô (“enclosure, pasture”). The second component, løk (“onion”), derives from Old Norse laukr (“leek, onion, garlic”), from Proto-Norse ᛚᚨᚢᚲᚨᛉ (laukaʀ, “leek”), from Proto-Germanic *laukaz (“leek, onion”). Their further origins are uncertain.
Compare the parallel formation Norwegian Nynorsk hagelauk (“onion”).
